Part 1 Assessment: The Riverside Cooking School

The assessment that closes Part 1 (Sessions 1 to 7), run in the second half of Session 7. Each learner works alone for 60 minutes, open book, in one SQL file on a database they have never seen: a fictional cooking school with instructors, classes and students. They build and protect the table that links students to classes, change data safely, and answer eight questions with filters, aggregates, subqueries and joins. Score it with the five-row rubric below. The instructor answer notes hold the reference output and what the common wrong answers print: this section is for instructors only.

Covers Modules 1–4Session 7, second half60 min in the roomOpen book, aloneMet: 14/20, no row at 1Instructor only

Part 1 Assessment: The Brief (as the Instructor Sees It)

Files. Learners get labs/module-07/part1-assessment/part1_assessment_starter.sql: the brief is its header and TODO comments, and running it builds kit_riverside (instructors 5 rows, classes 8, students 8), shows placeholder lines and drops the database at the end. Your reference is labs/module-07/part1-assessment/part1_assessment_solution.sql (never handed out before scoring). Both pass python3 labs/check_labs.py module-07. Programs that skip Session 7's assessment slot can run the same file as a take-home exercise (open book, 48 hours).

  • Deliverable: one file, part1_assessment_<name>.sql, that runs from start to finish with SOURCE and prints the answers (the starter's structure, every answer under its TODO; A3a's two errors written as comments).
  • Timing: 10 minutes of setup at 1:25 (rules, data, one run of the starter), 60 minutes of work (Part A about 20, Part B about 35, a final run 5), handed in at 2:35. Learners with agreed extra time get up to 30 more minutes, or finish the file at home within 48 hours.
  • Rules: open book (lesson pages, notes, workbook, own scripts); no other people, no AI assistants. Joins and subqueries are both accepted wherever both work; Part B is scored on the data AFTER Part A (a skipped Part A step changes later numbers; score each answer against what the learner's own file produced, see the notes).
  • Assessed: the submitted file against the five rubric rows. The Part 1 review that follows in the room is not scored.

Part 1 Assessment: The Rubric

Criterion1 · Beginning2 · Developing3 · Proficient4 · Exemplary
Table design and constraints (A1) · weight 20%No table, or a table without a primary key; keys missing.A table that loads the data, but with a single-column key (duplicates possible), keys unnamed or missing one side, or no CHECK; no reasons for the rules.Composite PRIMARY KEY (student_id, class_id); two named foreign keys referencing students(id) and classes(id); enrolled_on DATE NOT NULL; a CHECK that refuses 6; a delete rule per key with a one-sentence reason that fits it.Also matches column types exactly to the parents (INT), names every constraint, and the reasons weigh history against clean-up (for example RESTRICT for students, CASCADE for classes) or argue a different choice convincingly.
Data changes and integrity (A2, A3) · weight 15%UPDATE or DELETE without WHERE, or data loaded with checks switched off.The changes are made but A3a's errors are missing or misread (1451 for a missing student), or a change hits more rows than asked.A2 loads 15 rows (12 rated); A3a records 1452 (no such student) and 3819 (CHECK), each with what it means; one UPDATE with WHERE cuisine = 'Italian'; one DELETE by id; the class list shows 7 classes, Pasta 70.00 and Risotto 60.00.Also checks the effect of each change with a SELECT and explains why deleting class 8 is safe (no enrollments; or what CASCADE would do if it had some).
Filtering, sorting and aggregates (B1 to B4) · weight 25%Two or more of B1 to B4 missing or not running.Answers run but one or two are wrong: a missing date bound, AVG(COALESCE(rating, 0)), COUNT(*) for ratings, a missing tie-breaker, an aggregate in WHERE.All four right on the data after Part A: B1 Sourdough 45.00 and Tacos 50.00; B2 Italian and Japanese 65.00, Baking 60.00, Mexican 50.00; B3 Ana, Chloe, Emma with 3; B4 seven classes with blank ratings skipped (Pasta 3 / 2 / 4.5). Each has an ORDER BY.Also readable: aliases for every computed column, ROUND where a person reads the number, HAVING only for group conditions.
Subqueries and joins (B5 to B8) · weight 25%Two or more of B5 to B8 missing or not running.Answers run but one or two are wrong: a typed average in B5, an inner join or IS NULL after an inner join in B7, Nadia missing or a fan-out in B8.All four right: B5 French Pastry, Fresh Pasta by Hand, Sushi Basics; B6 five April enrollments with three names each; B7 Gina Russo and Hugo Weber; B8 five instructors from Marco Rossi 330.00 to Nadia Haddad 0.00. Joins or subqueries, both accepted.Also: qualified columns throughout, the anti-join or NOT EXISTS chosen deliberately, and B8's sum robust to a class with no enrollments (CASE or a count of enrollments times price).
Script quality (the whole file) · weight 15%The file does not run, or answers are not in the file.Runs only after edits, or stops partway; typed numbers where the database could compute them; no comments.Runs start to finish with SOURCE and no error; every answer under its TODO; ORDER BY whenever several rows come back; a comment where a choice was made.Also consistent formatting and aliases a reader can follow without the brief.
Scoring and the result
  • Score each row 1 to 4 (whole numbers). Report the total out of 20 and, if your program uses percentages, the weighted score (weights in the rubric: 20 / 15 / 25 / 25 / 15).
  • Part 1 met: a total of 14 or more and no row at 1. That is Proficient on most rows, with room for one Developing row.
  • Met after revision: a total of 11 to 13, or one row at 1 with a total of 14 or more. The learner fixes the weakest row's tasks in the same file within one week; re-score those rows only.
  • Not yet: a total of 10 or less, or two rows at 1. Return written feedback (one strength per row, the single change that would help most) and offer the take-home variant once, within two weeks.
  • Run before you read: SOURCE the file first. A file that stops with an error is scored on what it printed and on the code you can read; the Script quality row takes the hit, not the content rows twice.

Part 1 Assessment: Scoring Guidance by Row

RowWhat to look for
Table design and constraintsPRIMARY KEY (student_id, class_id) (a separate id column with no UNIQUE on the pair caps the row at 2: the "only once" rule is not enforced); two CONSTRAINT ... FOREIGN KEY lines with ON DELETE rules; CHECK (rating BETWEEN 1 AND 5) (or >= 1 AND <= 5); the two reason sentences. Any rule pair with a sensible reason is Proficient; CASCADE on students with no reason is Developing.
Data changes and integrityA3a's two comments name 1452 and 3819 and say what each means; the UPDATE has a WHERE on cuisine (or on ids 1 and 2); the DELETE removes id 8 only. Look for SET FOREIGN_KEY_CHECKS = 0 (caps the row at 1).
Filtering, sorting and aggregatesCompare B1 to B4 with the reference output below. B1 needs both date bounds (BETWEEN or >= and <) and price < 70; B4's average must skip blanks (AVG(rating)), and ratings given must be COUNT(rating).
Subqueries and joinsB5 with a subquery (a typed 61.43 prints the right rows today: Developing, see the traps); B7 with LEFT JOIN ... IS NULL, NOT EXISTS or NOT IN (safe here: student ids are never NULL); B8 must show Nadia Haddad with 0.
Script qualitySOURCE runs end to end; ORDER BY on every multi-row answer (B3 by last name, B6 by date, B8 by revenue then name); readable aliases; comments at the choices.

Part 1 Assessment: Instructor Answer Notes

A sound solution: steps
  • A1: a composite primary key, two named foreign keys (the reference: students RESTRICT, a paid booking is history; classes CASCADE, a cancelled class's bookings mean nothing without it), a CHECK, enrolled_on DATE NOT NULL, rating TINYINT nullable.
  • A2: turn on the INSERT; A3a: run the two statements at the prompt and copy the errors into comments; A3b: UPDATE classes SET price = price + 5.00 WHERE cuisine = 'Italian';; A3c: DELETE FROM classes WHERE id = 8;.
  • B1 to B4: WHERE, ORDER BY, GROUP BY, HAVING, COUNT(column) versus COUNT(*). B5: a scalar subquery. B6: four tables joined on their keys. B7: the anti-join. B8: LEFT JOIN from instructors to classes to enrollments, COUNT of an enrollment column, a sum that adds a price only for real enrollments.

Traps (and what they print)
  • Part A3 skipped, B1 run anyway: Fresh Pasta by Hand (65.00, not yet raised) joins the March list: three rows instead of two. Score B1 as right if the learner's own A3b is missing (score the missing A3b in its row), not twice.
  • B8 with SUM(c.price) and class 8 not deleted: Diego Morales shows 180.00 instead of 100.00 (the empty class's 80.00 is summed once from its NULL-padded row) and Marco Rossi 305.00 (prices not raised). With A3 done, SUM(c.price) happens to print the reference numbers: accept it as Proficient, and award Exemplary only for a sum that would stay right with an empty class.
  • B8 with inner joins: four instructors; Nadia Haddad (no classes) is missing. Developing on the joins row.
  • B4 with AVG(COALESCE(rating, 0)): blanks count as zero stars: Fresh Pasta by Hand 3.0 instead of 4.5, Sourdough Starter and French Pastry 2.5 instead of 5.0. Developing on the aggregates row.
  • B7 with an inner join and IS NULL: Empty set. An inner join has no unmatched rows.
  • B5 with the average typed in (WHERE price > 61.43): the same three classes today (the average after Part A is 61.43), wrong after the next price change. Developing on the joins/subqueries row, and note it under Script quality.
  • B3 or B6 with ambiguous columns: error 1052 stops the file at that query; the rest still runs if the learner turned it off. Script quality takes it.
What an honest result sounds like
  • A strong file reads like the reference: every answer under its TODO, a comment at A1's rules ("RESTRICT: a booking is a record of payment"), B8 with Nadia at 0.00.
  • Follow-up questions for the feedback or a short conversation: "Why can a student enroll in a class only once in your table?" · "What would B8 print if a class had no enrollments?" · "Which of your queries would break if a price changed tomorrow?"
  • A file with Part A complete and five of eight Part B answers right usually lands at 14 or 15: met. Part B answers that are wrong only because Part A was skipped are not penalized twice.

Part 1 Assessment: Accommodations, Late Work and Completion

  • Extra time: up to 30 minutes in the room, agreed before Session 7; or the take-home variant (the same file, 48 hours, open book).
  • Missed Session 7: the take-home variant within one week, plus a 10-minute conversation about two of the answers.
  • Academic honesty: discussion after hand-in is encouraged; shared files are not. You may ask any learner to explain two of their queries in five minutes; an answer they cannot explain is re-scored after a short redo.
  • Part 1 on its own: a learner completes Part 1 with the assessment met (or met after revision) and the seven sessions attended or made up. Checkpoint 1 (Session 4) is formative and not counted in the result; a "not yet" there predicts trouble in the aggregates row: visit those learners first during the assessment's Part B.
  • Part 2 follows: the Part 1 result is recorded beside the final project (Sessions 12 to 14); a "not yet" on Part 1 does not block Part 2, but the learner redoes the weakest row's tasks before Session 9.
